articles.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
articles.summary: Ukraine's president said allowing Russia to sell petroleum products would prolong a war that must be ended.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to the US and globally.

Trump said the proposed release of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, in tranches, would see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Ukraine's president criticised the decision, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war between the two countries.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

He added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.

Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.

The BBC has asked the White House for clarity on what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.

Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."

An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, and introduced a ban on diesel exports.

According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.

Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.

But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".

"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear.

But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.

What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.

With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.

Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.

Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

articles.title: Vance suggests Nidal Hasan’s execution won’t be livestreamed, contradicting Hegseth
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance suggested the federal government wouldn’t livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, contradicting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance suggested Friday that the federal government would not livestream its planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad, contradicting the plan announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “First of all, I’ve seen these announcements. I don’t know that that’s going to happen,” Vance told reporters while traveling to a campaign event in Ohio. He said that if the execution, which is scheduled for December, is livestreamed that he wouldn’t watch it. “But what I try to remind people is: look, this is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” the vice president said. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a shooting at Texas’ Fort Hood Army base in 2009. While visiting the USS Abraham Lincoln as it docked in San Diego on Thursday, Hegseth told conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice that Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.” It wasn’t immediately clear Friday why Vance contradicted Hegseth. The White House and Pentagon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. The decision to publicly show Hasan’s execution has been met with intense backlash from both some Republicans and many Democrats. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who has said he is considering a run for president in 2028, opposes broadcasting the execution. “If it were me, I wouldn’t televise it or publicize it or whatever they’re doing,” Kennedy said Friday while campaigning with GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Sterling Heights, Michigan. “I just think it makes — it makes our society coarser, and I wouldn’t do it. But there are arguments, you know, on both sides.” Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, wrote in a post on X Friday, “Seneca warned that Rome’s bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them. A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” he said. “Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.” Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., a frequent Trump critic, said in a post on X Thursday, “Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.” Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote, “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.” Rep. Ann Wager, R-Mo., wrote, “Justice will be served, but the United States of America does not and should not livestream executions.” Reps. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., and Tom Barrett, R-Mich., who are among the most vulnerable GOP members seeking re-election in November, posted similar sentiments on X. “Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision. Nidal Hasan is an evil person. He betrayed our country, killed 13 American soldiers, and wounded dozens more at Fort Hood — a place I trained the year before his brutal attack,” Barrett wrote. “That does not change the fact that our American values should strive to elevate human dignity. Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.” Bresnahan said the live stream should not happen. “The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he wrote. The military’s last execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old girl in Austria. The military last executed someone by firing in 1945, when it put Pvt. Eddie Slovik to death after he was court-martialed for desertion during World War II.

articles.title: Early vote analysis: Mail ballot concerns are changing how Democrats vote
articles.summary: Democrats are changing how they vote, requesting fewer mail ballots than in past elections but returning the ones they do request more quickly, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the early vote conducted in coordination with the University of Pennsylvania.
articles.body: Democrats are changing how they vote, requesting fewer mail ballots than in past elections but returning the ones they do request more quickly, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the early vote conducted in coordination with the University of Pennsylvania. The findings, which come less than four weeks before Election Day, reflect a midterm landscape shaped by concerns about mail-in voting and doubts about the reliability of the U.S. Postal Service. The shift among Democrats suggests they may be abandoning mail ballots in favor of in-person voting, or taking precautions to ensure their ballot arrives on time. The implications could be significant. Since 2020, Democrats have been far more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, creating predictable patterns in how early election tallies shift as additional votes are counted. But if those habits are changing, it will be more difficult to gauge which party has more enthusiasm from early voting figures, while the now-familiar red and blue “mirages” seen on recent election nights could unfold differently. For the analysis, we compared current and historical data on mail ballot requests and returns at the same point in time across four states: North Carolina, Georgia, Virginia and Pennsylvania. We gathered publicly available data from three states and sourced Virginia data from L2, a leading voter data firm. Trump order supercharges concerns about the Postal Service President Donald Trump has long attacked mail voting as rife with unfounded claims of fraud. Heading into the midterms, his administration exerted increased control over the Postal Service, whose slowed delivery times had already prompted voting rights groups and Democrats to push their voters to consider using other methods of voting. Just months before the first mail ballots of the midterm elections were scheduled to go out, the Postal Service followed a Trump directive to impose new rules about how election officials could send those ballots to voters. The new requirements will ultimately not apply to this year’s midterm election, but the high-profile legal battle magnified worries about the reliability of the Postal Service. Confidence that the Postal Service would deliver mail ballots on time plummeted among Democrats from 86% before the 2024 election to 60% now, according to polling conducted by Marist in September, just after the Supreme Court blocked the new Postal Service rules from going into effect. Confidence among Republicans remains unchanged. Meanwhile, more Democrats said they planned to vote in person this year than said the same at this time in 2024, according to NBC News polling. The early vote data we examined suggests that what these Democratic voters may actually do is dependent on when voters may request mail ballots in each state. In some states, voters may join a permanent list of mail voters or an annual list at the start of each year. If voters could request their ballot long before concerns about the Postal Service became national news, Democrats are still voting by mail, but taking steps to get those ballots back to election officials more quickly, the analysis shows. But if Democrats face the choice about whether to request a mail ballot only after the Postal Service challenges, it’s more likely that ballot requests are down from previous election years. Changing early voting patterns In North Carolina, where the Senate race is poised to help decide control of the chamber, registrants typically apply for a mail ballot in the months before each particular election. As a result, few individuals had requested mail ballots for the upcoming midterm before the Postal Service attempted to impose its new rules. So far, Democrats in the state are both less likely to request and more likely to return mail ballots compared to 2022, the most recent midterm election year. The decrease is larger among Democratic registered voters at 40% than among Republican registered voters or independent or third-party registrants at 18% and 23%, respectively. Further, the Democratic registrants who have requested mail ballots are more likely to have already returned them in 2026 (22%) than in 2022 (17%). In Georgia, a state with competitive Senate and gubernatorial contests and a similar mail ballot request policy, we see the same pattern. While it’s not possible to directly replicate the North Carolina analysis because registrants in the state do not declare a party of registration and domestic mail ballots only went out this week, we can use how each precinct voted in 2024 as an approximation of the partisanship of voters. As in North Carolina, the analysis shows that mail ballot requests are down more in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Kamala Harris (52%) than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Donald Trump (39%). The story is different in Virginia. Unlike North Carolina or Georgia, Virginia allows registrants to sign up for a permanent absentee mailing list, and a substantial share of returned mail ballots are cast by registered voters on this permanent list. As a result, there’s been no drop-off in mail ballot requests compared to the last general election held in the state. But as in Georgia and North Carolina, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster. In the most Democratic precincts, 69% more ballots were returned at this point in the 2026 election compared to 2025, compared to 5% fewer returned ballots in the most Republican precincts. One advantage of analyzing Virginia is that it is one of the few states with a significant amount of early in-person voting at this point in the electoral calendar. Relative to 2025, there are more early in-person ballots already cast in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Harris (+10%) in 2024 than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Trump (-14%). But only a small portion of this increase is caused by people shifting from voting by mail to voting early in person, so it does not explain most of the increase in early in-person voting. Still, the relatively higher rate of people voting early in person in Democratic precincts compared to Republican precincts suggests that most Democrats who are shifting away from mail balloting, including in North Carolina and Georgia, may move to voting in person rather than not voting at all. Finally, consider Pennsylvania, which maintains an annual list for mail ballot applications. Of the four states analyzed, it had the highest share of ballots cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election — 27%, versus Virginia at 11%, North Carolina at 5% and Georgia at 5%. When registrants request a mail ballot in Pennsylvania, they are permitted to request a mail ballot for every subsequent election in that calendar year. Many registrants who request a mail ballot for the May primary election also request a mail ballot for the upcoming general election. As in North Carolina and Georgia, there are fewer mail ballot requests from Democrats at this point in 2026 than in 2022. However, there is no difference among Democrats requesting mail ballots by May. Instead, the decline is concentrated among mail ballot requests after May, likely reflecting the increased uncertainty about the Postal Service since the summer. Further, consistent with the other findings, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster than in the past. A higher percentage of mail ballots requested by registered Democrats have already been returned (20%) than at this same point in 2022 (15%). Why changing voting habits could complicate election night analysis These changes in Democratic voting behavior present two challenges for election analysts: determining what the early vote data reveal about voter enthusiasm, and understanding what’s happening on election night as results are processed. At this point, it is difficult to use the initial mail ballot data to gauge each party’s likelihood of success. The relative decline in mail ballot requests could be interpreted as a sign that Democrats have less momentum heading into the midterm election than current polling indicates. But Democrats may also be shifting from voting by mail to voting in person, as the findings in Virginia suggest. Conversely, the relative increase in mail ballot returns among Democrats might mean the party’s voters are particularly enthusiastic about the upcoming election. But this pattern is also consistent with these Democrats returning their mail ballots faster to address concerns about Postal Service slowdowns. Observing who casts early in-person votes over the next several weeks will help test these competing narratives. Still, we won’t have a clear picture of voter enthusiasm until we see who turns out on Election Day. Beyond that, our findings underscore the need for caution when interpreting early voting data and election-night results. Analysts often rely on voting patterns from past elections as key benchmarks to assess how each party is performing on election night. But if more Democrats vote in person, or get those mail ballots in faster, the timing of when Democratic votes are reported and counted could change in important ways. Thus, what may seem to be either a Democratic over- or under- performance on election night could instead be the reflection of the election landscape shifting once more.

articles.title: Kash Patel announces arrest of suspected ShinyHunters co-conspirator after FBI jobs portal breach
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel says agents arrested a suspected ShinyHunters co-conspirator tied to the FBIjobs.gov data breach and third-party vendor hack.
articles.body: FBI Director Kash Patel announced Friday that agents arrested another suspected co-conspirator linked to the ShinyHunters hacking group earlier this week during the bureau's investigation of a cybersecurity incident involving its jobs website. The arrest is the latest in a series of FBI actions against the hacking network in recent days, according to Patel, who said investigators are pursuing additional leads and evidence. "Earlier this week, our agents in the field arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group, the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor," Patel said in an Oct. 9 statement. FBI INVESTIGATES AFTER SHINYHUNTERS HACKERS CLAIM THEFT OF AGENTS' PERSONAL DATA Patel said the FBI is working with its partners to dismantle the group and its associates. "This arrest demonstrates the strength and reach of our efforts to protect Americans from cybercrime. We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate." ShinyHunters, a criminal hacking and extortion group, previously said it obtained sensitive personal information belonging to FBI employees and applicants through the bureau's jobs portal.16-YEAR-OLD ALLEGEDLY LED RANSOMWARE GANG BEHIND HUNDREDS OF ATTACKS The group said it stole information belonging to nearly all FBI agents and people who applied to work for the bureau, Reuters previously reported. A sample of data shared with the outlet contained agents' names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, names of family members. The FBI previously said it was investigating whether the breach originated within its own systems or through a third-party provider supporting FBIJobs.gov. The extent of the alleged breach has not been independently confirmed. Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and CEO of Media Rep Global Strategies, previously told Fox News Digital the distinction between stolen personnel information and access to classified investigative systems is critical. FBI HACK CLAIM RAISES FEARS OVER SENSITIVE PERSONAL DATA "There is a meaningful difference between somebody obtaining personnel information and somebody gaining access to classified investigative systems," Pack said. "Based on what we know right now, there is no indication they have the keys to the kingdom." articles.title: Letitia James stumped by debate question while GOP rival delivers 'zinger for the ages'
articles.summary: Letitia James went silent for several seconds when asked to name a former AG she admired during the Thursday New York Attorney General debate.
articles.body: New York Democratic Attorney General Letitia James went silent for several seconds when asked to name a former state attorney general she admired during Thursday's New York attorney general race debate. "Tick tock," Errol Louis of Spectrum News 1, one of the moderators said to James, prompting laughter from the Attorney General. The attorney general's race in New York comes against the backdrop of James' ongoing dispute with President Donald Trump, who called James "a Complete and Total Disaster" and accused her of leading a "WITCH Hunt" against him in his endorsement of James' Republican challenger, Saritha Komatireddy, in August. LETITIA JAMES' UNDERDOG RIVAL TURNS AG'S OWN PLAYBOOK AGAINST HER WITH SCATHING 52-COUNT CAMPAIGN 'INDICTMENT' The pause from James drew immediate criticism from Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor and chief of staff for the Drug Enforcement Administration, who quipped from the podium that James "only admires herself." "An absolutely devastating moment for Tish James," conservative communications strategist Steve Guest wrote on X. "'She only admires herself' is a debate zinger for the ages." "No, no, no, no, we admire others," James said. "I admire all of the past attorney generals because it is a difficult job and you've got to stand up." When asked the same question, Komatireddy named Dennis Vacco, who served as the state's attorney general from 1995 to 1998. Like Komatireddy, he was also a former federal prosecutor. James then said that she admired former Democratic Attorney General Bob Abrams, who served from 1979 to 1993. The exchange, which came in the final moments of Thursday's debate, led critics to question whether James knew of other New York attorneys general. "Very telling moment," Steve McLaughlin, Rensselaer County executive, wrote on X. "James went completely blank because she's A: dumb as a rock B: has no idea who any former AG is because she's not doing the job and never has been." NY AG HOPEFUL BLASTS LETITIA JAMES AS MEDICAID FRAUD RECOVERIES COLLAPSE: 'SHE'S NOT DOING THE JOB' "She's a mouthpiece," McLaughlin continued. "Zero institutional knowledge." "Letitia James doesn't know the plural form of 'Attorney General,'" another Twitter user wrote. Nicole Kiprilov, a spokesperson for Komatireddy, echoed the candidate's comment on the debate stage. "Letitia James can’t name a single former Attorney General she admires because she’s too busy admiring herself. She’s turned the Attorney General’s office into her own political stage and ignored the safety of the state," Kiprilov said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "New Yorkers deserve a real prosecutor, not a joke like her!" But James' campaign pushed back on Komatireddy's characterization of James and how she runs her office. "Attorney General Letitia James spent much of the debate teaching her opponent how the Office of the Attorney General actually works, and she was happy to name former Attorney General Bob Abrams as someone she respects," a spokesperson for James said in a statement to Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER James' attorney general's office has been thrust into the national spotlight after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special investigator to examine an alleged gang rape that occurred at Cornell University in October 2024. The renewed attention comes in response to a recent lawsuit filed by the alleged victim, Jane Doe, against the university, the alleged perpetrators, her sorority and a bar that allegedly served her alcohol while she was underage. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But James has faced calls from an attorney for one of the defendants to recuse herself from the case over social media posts showing support for Jane Doe before James was appointed special investigator.

articles.title: Culture clash laid bare as violent Somali gangs grip suburban communities: ‘These kids are different’
articles.summary: Bloomington police say young Somali American gang members come from families with money, but investigators can't explain what drives the violence.
articles.body: More than 100 rounds fired in a Minnesota neighborhood have left police struggling to explain a troubling pattern: Somali American youths from financially comfortable households are turning online disputes into gang violence. The violence raises bigger questions about what is driving these gangs and whether struggles to fit into American life, cultural or clan ties, government policies or failures by schools and other institutions have played a role and what makes these youths different from traditional American street gangs. "They're coming from families. They got money, and they have resources," Bloomington Police Chief Booker Hodges told Fox News Digital of the young Somali American gang members under investigation. Those questions follow a late-night Bloomington gunfight that left one person injured during a string of shootings across suburban Minneapolis-St. Paul. 100-SHOT SOMALI GANG GUN BATTLE ROCKS MINNESOTA AS SHERIFF WARNS 'WE'RE IN TROUBLE' Hodges said the suspects defy traditional drug- or money-driven gang profiles. Asked what drives the violence beyond social media disputes, he acknowledged investigators lack a clear answer. "I don't know. I can't tell you. I really wish I could," Hodges said. Somalia, long considered a failed state until the mid-2010s, according to the U.N., has endured decades of clan-based warfare and weak central government authority, including the 1993 Battle of Mogadishu depicted in "Black Hawk Down," when Somali militiamen battled U.S. forces during an ill-fated military operation, part of the turmoil that drove waves of refugees to America.More than 111,000 Somali refugees were admitted to the U.S. between 2001 and 2023 through the federal refugee resettlement program, spanning the George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden administrations. Minnesota became a major destination, alongside sizable Somali American communities in New York, Texas and Ohio. Jessica Vaughan, director of policy studies at the Center for Immigration Studies, believes one possible explanation lies in how refugees have been resettled. "We have to remember also that this population's origins were as refugees who were a vulnerable population and traumatized in many cases," Vaughan told Fox News Digital. "But they were settled in clusters in certain places in the United States. And I believe that is a policy that has facilitated the formation of these gangs because it removes a lot of the incentives for people to assimilate. "And it just makes assimilation to the larger society much more difficult because it's not necessary for people to get by." Vaughan described an emphasis on preserving homeland cultures rather than encouraging integration as a "missed opportunity," arguing it can leave immigrants in a "separate society within the larger Minnesota community." History, however, complicates the argument that maintaining strong ethnic ties necessarily prevents assimilation. Stanford sociologist Tomás Jiménez cautioned against treating gang involvement among a small subset of second-generation immigrants as evidence that an entire community has failed to integrate. "I would actually not think of it as, like, a failed assimilation, as much as a particular kind of assimilation," Jiménez said. He noted that Italian, Irish, Mexican and Salvadoran communities experienced gang activity while broader integration continued. Jiménez emphasized that assimilation unfolds across generations, pointing out that the Italian American experience spanned roughly 75 years rather than occurring overnight. He identified education, economic advancement, language and intermarriage as important measures of integration. FOX NATION REVEALS HOW RUDY GIULIANI BROKE THE MAFIA'S GRIP ON NEW YORK Donald Tricarico, an Italian American immigration scholar at Queensborough Community College, drew parallels between Italian and Irish immigrants, who established close-knit ethnic communities in New York. He said Italian families often followed relatives from the same villages into the same neighborhoods and occupations. "They came to the same neighborhoods … what migration historians call 'chain migration,' and they ... went to the same neighborhoods," he said, citing his own family's multigenerational experience in New York City. "There isn't a switch that gets flipped," Tricarico said, challenging assumptions that Italian Americans assimilated quickly and noting that close-knit ethnic communities persisted into the 1980s in some cases. WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH "Assimilation is a slow crawl," he said, explaining that economic advancement and integration typically unfold across generations. Tricarico noted that some Sicilian immigrants arrived with ties to existing Mafia networks overseas, a criminal element distinct from the broader Italian immigrant population. Hodges, meanwhile, said investigators have found no evidence that longstanding clan rivalries in Somalia are driving the Minnesota violence. Somali American community figures have offered their own explanations, including the challenges facing immigrant parents. At an Eden Prairie news conference Wednesday, Somali teacher Fardousa Yossuf suggested parents working long hours may have neglected their children's needs and "expressed disbelief" that people raised with Islamic values could engage in gun violence, according to Alpha News. Imam Yusuf Abdulle rejected characterizing the violence as a Somali problem in an interview with WCCO - CBS Minnesota posted on YouTube. "These kids are Americans. They're born and raised here," Abdulle said. "It is an American problem. It is not a Somali problem." Vaughan, meanwhile, warned that the gangs have not reached the sophistication of transnational organizations such as MS-13 but could become more entrenched without intervention. She pointed to families and schools as critical to preventing recruitment and argued that local institutions and law enforcement must intervene before the groups become more organized. Vaughan acknowledged she had not established that specific Minnesota schools or resettlement policies prompted the shootings. Asked whether longstanding Somali clan rivalries were fueling the shootings, Hodges said investigators found no evidence supporting that explanation. "No, we have not seen that. I haven't seen it," he said. He added that people from groups in conflict in Somalia can belong to the same cliques in Minnesota. articles.title: State Department watchdog probing Kimberly Guilfoyle amid alleged $100,000 demand
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and the embassy she leads are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News.
articles.body: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and the embassy she leads are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News. The government watchdog’s probe comes as legal consultant and longtime Donald Trump supporter and donor Eric Deters has accused Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 confirmation hearing in exchange for access to senior administration officials. “She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview Thursday. “She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he said of Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, Trump campaign surrogate and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr. Deters provided NBC News with a PDF document of texts and Signal messages with Guilfoyle, which were first reported Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal. The Daily Mail first reported the watchdog investigation. One of the messages provided by Deters appears to show Guilfoyle instructing him to wire the money directly to American Express because “it won’t show up anywhere” that way. He said he did not pay her the money. An attorney for Guilfoyle did not respond to a request for comment, but told the Journal she disputed the authenticity of the messages while not providing specifics. Vice President JD Vance said Friday that “these are accusations” and “we don’t try people in the court of public opinion.” Deters’ claims, he said, are “one person’s story.” “Let’s actually see what the facts are. Let’s see what the truth is, and obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said. The White House had no comment. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last week asking for more information about additional allegations that appeared in The Wall Street Journal. On Thursday, Rubio chided a reporter for asking him about the accusations against Guilfoyle while he was with her in Athens. “We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you,” he said, adding: “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.” A senior diplomatic official, meanwhile, said the news of probe set off alarm bells throughout the State Department. The official described the investigation as rare and said that watchdog is known primarily for performing routine embassy inspections rather than investigations. A spokesperson for the State Department inspector general’s office said the watchdog does not confirm, deny or comment on investigations. The State Department declined to comment on the accusations against Guilfoyle or any investigation. Watchdog investigations into potential ethics violations by U.S. ambassadors are rare, but not unprecedented. During the first Trump administration, Woody Johnson, then the U.S. ambassador to the U.K. and a longtime Republican donor, was investigated by the State Department’s inspector general, who found he made “inappropriate” comments on race, gender and religion to embassy staff. The State Department rejected recommendations for Johnson, saying he had watched a government video on workplace harassment and instructed senior officials to do the same, and also encouraged staff to take a training course on “mitigating unconscious bias.” Under President Joe Biden in 2024, the watchdog investigated U.S. Ambassador to Singapore Jonathan Kaplan, finding the political appointee threatened his staff and failed to submit about $48,000 in travel expenses on time or with proper documentation. In Kaplan’s case, State said it was taking the recommendations seriously and made organizational changes. “The president always wants his representatives ... to manage people with dignity and respect,” former White House National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said at the time. “He’s comfortable that the State Department is taking this seriously.”

articles.title: Democrats’ mail ballot shift: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we dive into a shift in the way Democrats are casting their ballots so far ahead of the November election. Plus, Kristen Welker examines the key dynamics that were at play in last night’s Senate debates. — Adam Wollner Mail ballot concerns are changing how Democrats vote, early vote analysis shows By Michael Morse and Marc Meredith Democrats are changing how they vote, requesting fewer mail ballots than in past elections but returning the ones they do request more quickly, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the early vote conducted in coordination with the University of Pennsylvania. The findings, which come less than four weeks before Election Day, reflect a midterm landscape shaped by concerns about mail-in voting and doubts about the reliability of the U.S. Postal Service. The shift among Democrats suggests they may be abandoning mail ballots in favor of in-person voting, or taking precautions to ensure their ballot arrives on time. The implications could be significant. Since 2020, Democrats have been far more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, creating predictable patterns in how early election tallies shift as additional votes are counted. But if those habits are changing, it will be more difficult to gauge which party has more enthusiasm from early voting figures, while the now-familiar red and blue “mirages” seen on recent election nights could unfold differently. Take North Carolina, where the Senate race is poised to help decide control of the chamber. So far, Democrats in the state are both less likely to request and more likely to return mail ballots compared with 2022, the most recent midterm election year. The decrease is larger among Democratic registered voters, at 40% fewer mail ballots requested, than among Republican registered voters or independent or third-party registrants, at 18% and 23% fewer, respectively. Further, the Democratic registrants who have requested mail ballots are more likely to have already returned them in 2026 (22%) than in 2022 (17%). Confidence that the Postal Service would deliver mail ballots on time plummeted among Democrats from 86% before the 2024 election to 60% last month, according to polling conducted by Marist just after the Supreme Court blocked President Donald Trump’s new Postal Service rules from going into effect. By comparison, confidence among Republicans remains unchanged. Meanwhile, more Democrats said they planned to vote in person this year than said the same at this time in 2024, according to NBC News polling. Read more → What we learned from last night’s debates Analysis by Kristen Welker Debate season has reached a fever pitch just weeks before Election Day. And last night’s trio of Senate showdowns laid bare the dynamics and disagreements that will decide the fight for the majority. Arguably the biggest similarity across the three major Senate debates on Thursday — in Michigan, Maine and Georgia — underscores why Democrats believe they have the wind at their backs: They are all singing from the same songbook when it comes to the economy. In race after race, Democratic candidates are laying voters’ dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump at the feet of Republicans. Trump’s poor ratings on issues like the economy and immigration give these Democrats a clear opening as they call for change. And some Republican candidates have struggled to articulate how they will address these voter frustrations when they supported many of the president’s policies in the first place. But the personal attacks peppered throughout these debates reveal another important dynamic too: Republicans believe that in many cases, their best chance to swim against the political tide comes by making the campaign a referendum on the Democrat standing across from them, rather than Trump. Michigan’s heated Senate debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed may be the best example of this. The hourlong event featured no shortage of name-calling: Rogers’ repeated insistence that El-Sayed is a “con man” sought to undermine the Democrats’ economic attacks, while El-Sayed calling Rogers “weak” and “cowardly” aims to convince voters that the Republican won’t stand up to the president. It’s how both candidates closed their first debate. El-Sayed argued he was best positioned to stand up for Michiganders in Washington, while Rogers made the case that a vote for his opponent is too big of a risk. El-Sayed will join me on this Sunday’s “Meet the Press,” where we will dig deeper into the dynamics of this pivotal Senate race. I’ll also speak with retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and author Michael Lewis, to discuss their new books and how they are digesting the first two years of this Trump administration. 🗣️ Related read: In three separate debates this week, GOP candidates revealed when pushed on high costs that they’ve been in direct contact with Cabinet officials in the Trump administration to try to address them, Bridget Bowman notes. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: James Talarico back on the trail after an absence with the flu drew scrutiny
articles.summary: After drawing scrutiny for his absence from the campaign trail, Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, who had been sick with the flu, returned to the stump.
articles.body: After drawing scrutiny for his absence from the campaign trail, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who had been sick with the flu, returned to the stump in Texas on Friday. “James Talarico is back on the campaign trail talking to voters at Austin City Limits,” Talarico campaign spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. Social media posts showed Talarico walking on the grounds of the festival on Friday. Talarico revealed on Sept. 30 that he was sick, when he had to appear virtually instead of in person at a forum. His prolonged absence drew daily scrutiny from his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton’s campaign asked for “proof of life” and called on Talarico to produce a photo of himself and a newspaper with a current date. Republican Sen. Ted Cruz poked fun on social media, featuring a milk carton with Talarico’s face with the word “MISSING.” Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser and, according to his virtual remarks to the Hispanic Business Council the following day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care. Then, Talarico appeared visibly ill, blowing his nose and coughing through the event. “I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.” His absence from the trail in the crunch time of the election prompted some consternation among Democrats. “Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

articles.title: Trump selects Katie Zacharia as next White House press secretary
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has selected Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked briefly at the Department of Homeland Security, as his new press se...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has selected Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked briefly at the Department of Homeland Security, as his new press secretary.

Zacharia thanked Trump in a social media post Friday, writing, "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."

In announcing her selection earlier Friday, Trump highlighted her work for Truth Social, the Trump Media & Technology Group and her frequent appearances on Fox and Newsmax.

"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," he added.

Trump in recent days called a number of his close allies and advisers, including former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to seek their opinion of Zacharia, a person familiar with the discussions said. And the president sought Leavitt's counsel before making a final decision and offering Zacharia the position, they said.

CNN has reached out to Zacharia, who was in the Oval Office with Trump earlier Friday morning, according to a person familiar.

Zacharia's selection came about quickly. As of last week, she was not being considered for the role, another person familiar said.

Throughout the search to replace Leavitt, the White House struggled with higher-profile names, several of whom had previously criticized Trump. On multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list, only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position, according a White House official.

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," Zacharia wrote on X.

"I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out," she said, adding that "following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting."

Zacharia's been a frequent guest on Fox, Newsmax and CNN.

"She's a friend of most of you," Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Friday. "I know she likes people — she likes all of you. Actually, I don't know if that's good or bad, but we just hired a new press secretary, and she's going to be, I think, terrific."

Zacharia served as a senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group and Truth Social since June, which followed a two-month stint as a senior official at the Department of Homeland Security — experiences that Trump also highlighted in his social media post, along with her work in his campaigns.

Zacharia, who has young children and lives in California, commuted back and forth to Washington when she was filling in at DHS. At the time, she told a friend the commute was not sustainable, according to a source familiar with the matter.

Zacharia has also served as a legal adviser for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell.

She first came to Washington as an intern for the Republican National Committee during the George W. Bush administration in 2006.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

articles.title: AIPAC’s super PAC starts spending again in the Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: A super PAC tied to the pro-Israel group AIPAC has resumed spending in Michigan’s critical Senate race, funding new mailers targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, according to a new campaign finance report.
articles.body: A super PAC tied to the pro-Israel group AIPAC has resumed spending in Michigan’s critical Senate race, funding new mailers targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, according to a new campaign finance report. The group, United Democracy Project, hadn’t been involved in the general election despite spending millions to oppose El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, in the Democratic primary in August. The group filed a report with the Federal Election Commission on Friday showing that it spent $95,000 on mailers opposing El-Sayed. The group is targeting 130,000 Jewish voters with mailers, according to spokesperson Patrick Dorton. The mailer features a headline about an attack on a Michigan synagogue in March, which the FBI described as “Hezbollah- inspired act of terrorism.” “Abdul El-Sayed’s response: ‘Hurt people hurt people,’” the mailer reads, according to a copy shared with NBC News. El-Sayed apologized in late August for his response to the attack, saying his comments “may have been misconstrued to justify something I did not mean to justify.” The new spending is just a fraction of the $33 million United Democracy Project spent on ads in the Democratic primary against El-Sayed and in support of his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed has accused Israel of committing a genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed is now facing off against former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who has slammed his opponent for his positions on Israel. During their first debate Thursday night, Rogers said he would welcome AIPAC’s involvement when asked about an Axios report that the former congressman’s allies had asked the group to stay out of the race. “Anybody that wants to help my campaign stop a guy who can’t condemn terrorism in our own country because he’s so close to the people who are supporting the Muslim Brotherhood, again, I’ll take all of that help,” Rogers said. El-Sayed interjected to say, “Again, I’ve condemned them.” El-Sayed was asked during the debate whether he would support funding for defensive weapons for Israel if the country was attacked. “I don’t want our tax dollars buying weapons for other countries. I don’t know what’s so hard about that,” El-Sayed responded. He was also whether Iran or Israel posed a bigger threat to the United States, and declined to answer, calling the question “a ridiculous hypothetical.” “I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in a war with Iran,” El-Sayed said. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”

articles.title: US judge rules Trump administration’s use of voter data unlawful
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled against the Justice Department’s use of voter data to cross-reference an immigration database.
articles.body:
A United States judge has ruled that the Justice Department unlawfully sought state voter rolls to cross-check against a federal immigration database and identify voters it considered ineligible.

US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s decision on Friday marks another setback for President Donald Trump’s efforts to expand federal oversight of elections ahead of the midterms, as Republicans seek to retain control of Congress.

In a 78-page ruling siding with watchdog group Common Cause, Sooknanan said the administration had understated the risk of wrongly removing eligible citizens from voter rolls because of inaccuracies in the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database.

“The challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote,” Sooknanan wrote, adding that Congress had left that authority to the states.

The Justice Department said it was reviewing the ruling.

Ming Cheung, a senior staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Project, said the ruling made clear that the administration could not use the federal government to disrupt elections or put voters’ rights at risk.

“The Trump administration has repeatedly taken extreme measures to interfere with how elections are run, undermine confidence in the results, and create confusion,” Cheung said in a statement.

Last year, Trump directed the department to crack down on voting by ineligible people, despite research showing voter fraud is rare. The department subsequently demanded unredacted voter rolls from nearly all 50 states, including sensitive personal information.

Eighteen states, mostly Republican-led, complied. The department cross-checked their data against SAVE and flagged people identified as noncitizens for potential removal from voter rolls.

Sooknanan said the database could contain outdated citizenship records, potentially misidentifying naturalised US citizens.

The department has also sued 30 states and Washington, DC, over their refusal to provide voter data. Twenty-six cases have been dismissed.

In a separate case in June, Sooknanan blocked the expanded use of the SAVE database for voter roll checks, an order the US Supreme Court temporarily paused last month.

Federal law bars systematic voter roll purges in the 90 days before a federal election, which could limit the ruling’s practical effect before the November 3 vote.

articles.title: Trump picks "loyal" Katie Zacharia as next White House press secretary
articles.summary: "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary," President Trump said.
articles.body:
Washington — President Trump on Friday announced conservative commentator Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, praising her "unblemished record of support."

Zacharia, a California native, briefly worked for the Department of Homeland Security as a spokesperson earlier this year, and currently works as a senior communications adviser for Truth Social, the president's social media site. She also assisted the president on the campaign trail, he said.

"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," the president wrote on Truth Social. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA! I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."

The president wished her luck. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia was offered the role.

The position has been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left in late August. The White House James S. Brady Press Briefing Room hasn't hosted a briefing for the press since Sept. 3, when Vice President JD Vance addressed reporters and took questions.

In a social media post , Zacharia said "serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," she said in the post. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting."

Zacharia, who lives in California, completed her undergraduate and law degrees at Pepperdine University in Malibu, according to her LinkedIn.

Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed for the New York Post about her experience wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym. She said the owner of the gym ultimately asked her to stop wearing it.

"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door."

"The First Amendment has no 'discomfort' clause," she added, although the First Amendment protects against government censorship of speech, not private businesses.

articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
articles.summary: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
articles.body:
Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.

Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump's announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it "absolutely terrible" and "not fair and not honest".

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington's Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

"I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote.

"Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel."

He added: "Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority."

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran's closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November's midterm approach.

Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.

"This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries," the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. "Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia's war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas."

Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.

"Propping up Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities," congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X . "The President's policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity."

Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible." The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged". Russia was likely to repay it with "further terror and perfidy".

"It plays into Russia's hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine's embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been "used as a smokescreen for the deal", which he called "a weak decision by strong partners".

"That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington's Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance's resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy's relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: "You don't have the cards."

But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump's willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia's support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

images.caption: Trump in Washington on Wednesday. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

articles.title: Trump takes suit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
articles.summary: Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clint...
articles.body:
Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to ‌Russia.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers ‌for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the ​Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.

Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims.

Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.

US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, ‌and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller ⁠documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax."

Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year's ⁠election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.

US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump's lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him."

Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and ​his ​lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the ​sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly ‌advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts."

Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories.

The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.

"Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated.

In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the decisions by the lower courts are having a "profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole."

Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in ‌sweeping and systematic fashion," but stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign ​conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities."

Mueller said in his report that he ​found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia's effort ​to tilt the ballot in Trump's favor.

Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential ‌missteps by the FBI.

In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the ​FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential ​campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump's political opponents to fuel the probe.

Trump's Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. ​A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor ‌who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.

Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of ​the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump's campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, ​all of which Trump denied.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title: Bancadas na Câmara e no Senado: PL cresce e outros partidos encolhem | G1
articles.standfirst: Partido Liberal (PL) foi o que mais aumentou as bancadas na Câmara e no Senado; União Brasil, PSDB e PSD estão entre os que encolheram.
articles.summary: O PL amplia bancadas na Câmara e no Senado, enquanto União Brasil, PSDB e PSD registram as maiores perdas de espaço para a próxima legislatura.
articles.body:
As eleições de 2026 redistribuíram as cadeiras na Câmara dos Deputados e no Senado , com avanço do PL e perdas para partidos tradicionais. Enquanto o PL ampliou as bancadas nas duas Casas e se consolidou como a maior força parlamentar, siglas como PSD , União Brasil e PSDB reduziram sua representação, e o Cidadania ficou sem deputados eleitos para a próxima legislatura.

Na Câmara dos Deputados, o PL ampliou a bancada em 23 cadeiras e chega a 121 deputados na próxima legislatura; no Senado Federal, passa a ter 28 senadores.

Na Câmara, o avanço do PL ocorreu com folga sobre os demais partidos. PT e Novo aparecem em seguida, ambos com crescimento de cinco cadeiras. Enquanto o PT passou de 65 para 70 deputados, o Novo dobrou sua representação, chegando a 10 parlamentares — o maior crescimento proporcional, em relação aos deputados eleitos em 2022. PRD , PSOL e PV também registraram aumento de bancada, embora em menor escala.

Na outra ponta, União Brasil e PSDB foram as siglas que mais perderam espaço na Câmara. Os dois partidos encolheram em seis cadeiras. O União Brasil passou de 52 para 46 deputados, e o PSDB caiu de 17 para 11, registrando uma das maiores retrações proporcionais entre os partidos.

O saldo do Cidadania pós-eleições é significativo: o partido não terá representantes na Câmara em 2027.

Mudanças de cadeiras na Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: Arte/g1

Mantiveram o tamanho da bancada de uma legislatura para a outra o Podemos , PCdoB , Avante e Missão . Mas isso não significa que esses partidos permaneceram com todos os mesmos deputados.

No Podemos, dos 27 deputados que hoje estão na bancada, 12 foram reeleitos para a próxima legislatura. O mesmo ocorreu com 7 dos 11 deputados do PCdoB, 4 dos 5 deputados do Avante e o único deputado do Missão.

PL avança também no Senado; PSD registra a maior perda

No Senado, o PL também ampliou a bancada e chegou a 28 senadores, tornando-se o partido com maior presença na Casa.

Os ganhos mais expressivos depois do PL ficaram com Novo e União Brasil, que conquistaram três cadeiras cada. A Rede também ampliou sua representação, enquanto PT e PDT mantiveram o mesmo tamanho de bancada.

O levantamento combina os 54 senadores eleitos em 2026 com os ocupantes previstos das 27 cadeiras cujos mandatos terminam em janeiro de 2031. O mandato de senador é de oito anos e a Casa tem 81 cadeiras no total.

Mudanças de cadeiras no Senado Federal — Foto: Arte/g1

O PSD registrou a maior redução entre todas as legendas, com queda de nove cadeiras. A bancada passará a contar com cinco senadores em 2027. O PSB perdeu três vagas, enquanto PP e PSDB tiveram redução de duas cadeiras cada.

MDB , Republicanos , Podemos e Avante também encolheram, com perda de um representante. Apesar da redução em algumas siglas, o redesenho do Senado foi menos pulverizado do que o observado na Câmara, concentrando os maiores ganhos em poucos partidos.

articles.title: Saiba quem é a primeira vice-governadora da história do RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Silvana Covatti, do PP, é deputada estadual de cinco mandatos, compõe tradicional família da política gaúcha e também já foi primeira mulher a comandar a secretaria da Agricultura e presidente a Assembleia.
articles.summary: Silvana Covatti, do PP, é deputada estadual de cinco mandatos, compõe tradicional família da política gaúcha e também já foi primeira mulher a comandar a secretaria da Agricultura.
articles.body:
Silvana Covatti — Foto: Mateus Bruxel/Grupo RBS

No domingo (4), o Rio Grande do Sul elegeu sua primeira vice-governadora da história. Silvana Covatti (PP) compõe a chapa de Luciano Zucco (PL) que saiu vitoriosa das urnas em 1º turno.

Integrante da família Covatti, tradicional no Rio Grande do Sul, e do PP, o maior partido municipalista do estado, com 164 prefeitos eleitos em 2024 , Silvana rompeu algumas marcas em solo gaúcho.

Ela foi a primeira mulher a se tornar presidente da Assembleia Legislativa, em 2016 , e a primeira a conduzir a Secretaria Estadual da Agricultura, durante o governo Eduardo Leite (PSD). Agora, se torna a primeira vice-governadora.

"A candidatura como vice-governadora foi fundamental. Hoje, somos 52%, o voto feminino. E pela primeira vez vamos ter uma mulher ao lado de um homem para governar o estado", celebra Silvana.

"Esse olhar que eu vou ter ao lado do Zucco é muito importante. Um olhar de mulher para as pessoas, para as famílias gaúchas, para a saúde, para a educação . E o Zucco é um homem muito guerreiro, disciplinado. Tenho certeza que vamos honrar cada voto que os gaúchos e as gaúchas deram para o Zucco e a Silvana", completa.

Sua carreira política começa ao lado do marido, Vilson Covatti , ex-deputado estadual, federal e secretário de estado, que também participou de gestão Leite no Palácio Piratini. Silvana dedicou-se aos bastidores da política por 23 anos, assumindo, nesse período, a presidência o PP Mulher no RS, uma instância interna do partido.

Silvana concorreu pela primeira vez a uma vaga na Assembleia em 2006 , quando foi eleita a parlamentar mais votada entre as mulheres da 52ª legislatura, com 65.547 votos.

Em 2010 , a deputada foi reconduzida ao cargo com 85.604 votos, a maior votação do Legislativo gaúcho naquele ano.

Nas últimas eleições, em 2014 , superou mais uma vez sua própria votação com a conquista de 89.130 votos, sendo eleita a mais votada da bancada progressista no Parlamento gaúcho.

Em 2018 , voltou à Assembleia Legislativa, eleita com 75.068 votos, conquistando a quinta maior votação no estado. Na eleição passada, em 2022 , ficou em quarto lugar com 82.717 votos, conquistando seu quinto mandato no Parlamento gaúcho.
