articles.title: De desilusão com a política a viagens: abstenção nas eleições de 2026 é a maior desde 1998 | G1
articles.standfirst: Mais de 33 milhões de pessoas não foram às urnas no primeiro turno; proporcionalmente, eleitores do Sudeste e Centro-Oeste são os mais faltosos
articles.summary: Mais de 33 milhões de pessoas não foram às urnas no primeiro turno; proporcionalmente, eleitores do Sudeste e Centro-Oeste são os mais faltosos
articles.body:
O primeiro turno das eleições terminou com 33 milhões de brasileiros deixando de exercer o direito ao voto. Em uma eleição acirrada como a presidencial, a abstenção impacta diretamente nos resultados: foram 21,08% dos brasileiros que deixaram de votar neste ano.

O percentual dos eleitores que não votaram é o maior para o primeiro turno presidencial desde as eleições de 1998 . Naquele ano, com a reeleição de Fernando Henrique Cardoso (FHC), 21,49% dos eleitores faltaram à eleição.

Depois disso, houve uma recuperação, com mais brasileiros indo às urnas escolher não só seus presidentes, como governadores, senadores, deputados federais e estaduais.

Mas em 2018, o percentual de brasileiros que preferiram não exercer o direito ao voto ultrapassou 20% e tem crescido pouco a pouco nos últimos pleitos.

O eleitor que não votar no primeiro turno pode sim votar no segundo , já que, para a Justiça Eleitoral, cada turno é um novo pleito e, portanto, faltar ao primeiro não impede que o eleitor vote no segundo .

🔎No Brasil, o voto é obrigatório para cidadãos maiores de 18 anos e menores de 70 alfabetizados, segundo a Constituição Federal.

Os motivos para um eleitor deixar de comparecer na chamada "festa da democracia" são variados. Mas uma marca que permeou essa eleição foi o desânimo da população.

Para Murilo Medeiros, cientista político da Universidade de Brasília (UnB), o desânimo tem como um dos motivos a polarização. Com os dois principais candidatos, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), com altos índices de rejeição, há um "ambiente de desalento" com a política.

"A percepção de que o voto já não é capaz de produzir mudanças concretas favorece o afastamento do eleitor das urnas. A abstenção elevada é um sinal desse distanciamento entre a política e o eleitor", diz Medeiros.

Entre os 33 milhões deste ano, o g1 ouviu relatos de eleitores de diferentes idades, profissões e contextos. Veja abaixo:

Burocracia e falta de acessibilidade afastam eleitores

Roberto Gepp, estudante de economia, diz que gostaria de ter votado, mas acabou não transferindo o título de eleitor. Ele se mudou de Brasília para São Paulo e também não poderá votar no segundo turno.

Para ele, foi uma “pena” não escolher seus representantes e afirma que o processo de transferência do título afasta e burocratiza o voto.

🔎O prazo para transferir o local de votação terminou no dia 6 de maio. No entanto, até o dia 20 de agosto, eleitores que estivessem fora do domicílio eleitoral no dia das eleições poderiam solicitar a alteração temporária do local de votação para votar em trânsito.

Ao se deparar com muitas pessoas e uma zona eleitoral que considerou desorganizada, Henrique Eduardo Bahouth, 73 anos, desistiu de votar.

“Eu nunca deixei de votar. Esse ano, realmente, eu ainda cheguei na minha zona eleitoral, mas estava cheia de muitas pessoas, achei muito desorganizado e eu, em função até do dia, eu não estava bem e acabei desistindo”, disse.

Já Bianca Dantas não conseguiu votar por uma questão de acessibilidade na seção em que iria votar. Ela conta que, após passar por uma cirurgia no joelho duas semanas antes do primeiro turno, não conseguiu chegar à seção eleitoral.

Ao chegar ao local e se deparar com dois lances de escada, precisou ir embora sem votar. Ela explica que não teve tempo de solicitar uma seção com acessibilidade.

“Quantas pessoas deixaram de votar por essa mesma razão, né? Pessoas que sofreram acidentes, enfim, e isso foi muito frustrante para mim, assim, ter que virar, estar ali na porta e ter que virar as costas e ir embora sem poder votar”, questionou.

Ceará registra menor abstenção do país com 15,5% no 1º turno das eleições de 2026. — Foto: Fabiane de Paula/ SVM

Aos 73 anos, Maria Luíza Teixeira tem o direito de deixar de votar, mas afirma que não compareceu às urnas no primeiro turno por discordar dos dois candidatos à Presidência, Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro.

Ao g1, Maria Luíza disse que também não pretende votar no segundo turno e que, se comparecesse às urnas, anularia o voto.

Desanimada com a política, a servidora pública Nara Oliveira afirmou que para ela não valia a pena gastar tempo e dinheiro com o deslocamento até o local de votação.

Nara citou o caso do Banco Master para explicar por que acredita que os políticos pensam apenas nos próprios interesses. Na avaliação dela, a eleição resume o significado da expressão “tanto faz”.

“Qualquer um que ganhar vai pensar só nos interesses próprios, e não vale a pena eu perder um segundo sequer da minha vida para votar em ninguém”, afirmou.

Já a estudante Maria Júlia Costa viajou para uma cidade distante daquela onde vota durante o primeiro turno para um evento de família e disse que pretende participar da votação no segundo turno.

A estudante afirmou ainda que acredita “na política, no poder do voto e na cidadania”.

A abstenção de 21,08% deste ano seguiu o ritmo de crescimento da ausência no primeiro turno dos últimos anos. Em 2022, o segundo turno não teve um movimento para que mais pessoas fossem às urnas escolher um presidente, segundo dados do TSE.

Ainda assim, levar esses eleitores a reconsiderarem e votarem é uma das estratégias de comunicação do presidente Lula, que saiu em desvantagem da primeira etapa de votação. Medeiros indica que esse será um dos maiores desafios a partir de agora.

"O segundo turno acende um alerta ainda maior para a abstenção. Com 21 governos estaduais definidos, a eleição presidencial será a única disputa em grande parte do país", explica o cientista político.

"Isso esvazia a mobilização política nos estados, desestimula o engajamento das lideranças locais e enfraquece as estruturas de campanha responsáveis por levar o eleitor às urnas", disse Medeiros.

Dados do TSE mostram que os maiores percentuais de eleitores que deixaram de votar são das regiões: 15 milhões de eleitores do Sudeste (22,7%) e 2,6 milhões do Centro-Oeste (21,7%).

"Aumentar o comparecimento, portanto, não significa aumentar os votos de Lula. Tudo depende do perfil político de quem ficou em casa", afirmou Medeiros.

Já no Nordeste, região que votou em sua maioria em Lula, 18,4% dos eleitores deixaram de comparecer às urnas. O contingente representa 8 milhões de eleitores.

Levar esse eleitor às urnas, no entanto, representa um desafio para as campanhas que buscam ampliar o número de votos.

"Embora o voto seja obrigatório no Brasil, a multa pelo não comparecimento é irrisória. O custo e as dificuldades para chegar às urnas, especialmente para eleitores de renda mais baixa, superam o valor da própria penalidade", explica.

articles.title: GOP priorities alienate MAHA supporters
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story GOP priorities alienate MAHA supporters Supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda are feeling betrayed by the Republican Party as the administration cozies up to industry insiders and lawmakers support legislation contrary to their values. © AP Photo/Jacquelyn…
articles.body:
Supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda are feeling betrayed by the Republican Party as the administration cozies up to industry insiders and lawmakers support legislation contrary to their values.

At last week’s MAHA summit, industry insiders representing artificial intelligence, big business and the pharmaceutical industry were given the stage alongside top Trump administration officials. Less represented at the event were MAHA activists.

Voters in this bloc are characterized by their support for Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as well as distrust of vaccine mandates and chemical and agriculture corporations .

“Do we vote for someone who supports vaccine mandates … or do we vote for someone who is actively supporting pesticides and poison in our foods that our babies and children eat on a daily basis?” said Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America. “It’s an impossible decision, and this is why many of our moms are saying they’re going to stay home, or vote independent, write somebody in.”

MAHA supporters were left disappointed earlier this year when the GOP’s farm bill included provisions to extend the deadline for the EPA to re-review health impacts of pesticides that are already on the market.

For pesticides that were on the market prior to a 2007 update to the law, the deadline had previously been 2026. The farm bill would extend it to 2031 .

Jeff Hutt, who worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign, agreed that many of the MAHA supporters who backed Trump in 2024 specifically because of Kennedy may stay home . Republicans shouldn’t count on those votes, he said, because the party is more beholden to Trump than to the MAHA ideals.

“The Republican Party really went from being a big tent party in ‘24 to a pup tent party in ‘26. I think a lot of those voters are going to stay home,” said Hutt.

articles.title: James Talarico resurfaces after extended absence as his campaign pushes back
articles.summary: James Talarico resurfaces at Austin City Limits after a 12-day absence that drew sharp attacks from Trump and Ken Paxton on the campaign trail.
articles.body: Texas Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico reappeared on the campaign trail Friday after a nearly two-week absence, ending days of speculation and criticism from political opponents regarding his whereabouts. "Hate to disappoint the conspiracy theorists, but James is still alive and meeting with voters at ACL today," Talarico’s primary spokesperson, JT Ennis, wrote on X. The post included a video of the candidate walking through crowds and greeting supporters at the Austin City Limits Music Festival. MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD Talarico, who is challenging Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a closely watched U.S. Senate contest, had not been seen publicly in person at a campaign event since late September. His last in-person event was a Sept. 26 news conference in Carrollton addressing rising gas prices. Talarico's campaign attributed the absence to a severe case of the flu. However, the prolonged pause drew sharp criticism from Republicans, including President Donald Trump. HECKLERS INTERRUPT TRUMP TEXAS RALLY MULTIPLE TIMES In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the Democrat was "MISSING IN ACTION." "TalaFREAKo has been missing for 12 days! Now, after looking for him throughout all of Texas, and beyond, probably even weirder places than anyone would think possible, he put out a statement that he has the 'flu,'" Trump wrote. "12 days is a long time to rid yourself of the so-called flu bug. What’s going on?" he added. "We need a Senator that’s a proven Champion like one that has been, without question, the Greatest Attorney General in the History of Texas, and one of the Greatest in the U.S.A." Talarico’s campaign pushed back on the characterization that he had been absent from the campaign trail for nearly two weeks, saying he attended a Zoom on Sept. 30 with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council after canceling an in-person event. The campaign argued that because he attended that Zoom, his absence was closer to nine days. COWBOYS LEGEND RANDY WHITE ENDORSES KEN PAXTON, WARNS JAMES TALARICO ‘CAN’T BE TRUSTED’ Talarico's last public event was a Sept. 26 campaign event in Texas, where he held a news conference in Carrollton. On Sept. 28, he attended a fundraiser in New York City. The next day, he said he'd been diagnosed with the flu. Talarico's absence also prompted Paxton to target his opponent’s absence while on the campaign trail. "Where is James Talarico?" Paxton asked during a campaign rally in San Antonio. PAXTON VENTS OVER LACK OF CAMPAIGN CONTROL AS DC ESTABLISHMENT HE ONCE BATTLED COMES TO HIS AID Talarico's campaign confirmed he expects to return to a full in-person schedule through the weekend ahead of an Oct. 14 CNN town hall. articles.title: Trump thinks he should have won the Nobel Peace Prize. His quest for it is now the butt of the joke
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is enduring his second straight Nobel loss.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is enduring his second straight Nobel loss.

"The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said at a rally in Syracuse, New York, late Friday night, devoting a remarkable amount of time to discussing the prize that was awarded earlier in the day to South African human rights pioneer Navi Pillay .

The president called it an "indelible stain on the country of Norway" and said he'd never heard of this year's winner. (The prize is not awarded by the Norwegian government.)

But Trump's quixotic quest for his own Nobel — which included effectively coercing last year's winner to give him her medal earlier this year— was the butt of a joke for the latest winner on Friday.

"If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump ," Pillay quipped to an applauding crowd.

The indignity for Trump caps what is now clearly a lost cause.

But his campaign for the Nobel epitomizes the problems of his second term: He seeks personal glory, but he's all too eager to try and take shortcuts to get there. And strewn along the path are haphazard and often counterproductive gambits.

He brought up the award repeatedly, effectively launching his a lobbying campaign on behalf of himself.

His main claim for why he deserved the award — that he settled more than half a dozen wars — is simply false, as CNN has noted .

Trump drove home how bizarre that claim was when he repeatedly misstated the names of the countries whose wars he supposedly settled.

Trump didn't even convince much of his own base; a Washington Post poll last year found just 22% of Americans and 49% of Republicans said he deserved the prize.

Talk of a legitimate Trump claim to a Nobel briefly perked up when a phase-one ceasefire deal was reached in Gaza.

But even by that point, the Trump administration was also doing something that seemed quite problematic: It was killing people — alleged drug-traffickers, it has said — without due process on the open seas. Many experts have regarded these as extrajudicial killings that could amount to war crimes.

Also at that time, Trump had dispatched the US military to several places across the country — in some cases illegally, it turned out.

When Trump didn't win the Nobel last year, FIFA created its own peace prize and bestowed it on him in a transparent effort to curry favor with the president. (The ceremony was a sight to behold.)

But the whole charade really fell apart early this year.

That's when Trump ramped up his talk about taking over Greenland. He even left open the possibility of taking it by force — effectively threatening an invasion of a NATO ally (although he later backed off that effort).

He actually did invade Venezuela to arrest Nicolás Maduro. The White House might argue this was a humanitarian mission to free the Venezuelan people of an evil, criminal dictator. But Trump left the rest of the regime in power and has since pitched the invasion as an effective seizure of Venezuelan resources (read: oil). He even summarized the operation thusly last month at the United Nations General Assembly: " To the victor belong the spoils ."

That is not a phrase associated with the average Nobel Peace Prize winner. And he repeated it Friday night, adding, "We're taking out for ourselves — we deserve it."

A couple weeks after the invasion, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado gave him her medal , apparently hoping it would convince Trump to more strongly support her cause. It has not worked.

And then Trump in February launched a war against Iran, based on inconsistent and highly suspect claims , that has much of the world crying foul. The war, which has now stretched more than seven months, almost certainly eliminated any hope Trump had of winning a Nobel.

That's really the story here: Trump looking for his Nobel in all the wrong places — and constantly shooting himself in the foot in the process.

If the president wanted a Nobel prize, it might have behooved him to try and hue a more closely to international law and not kill people who aren't part of an armed conflict on the high seas. He might also not want to spend time cracking down on the opposition within the US while threatening and launching foreign invasions.

And after failing to end a Russia-Ukraine war that he assured he could end on Day One of his presidency, Trump instead repeatedly exaggerated his role in ending wars. (And in some cases, they weren't even actual wars.)

Then, when he didn't win the Nobel last year, he got other people to give him consolation prizes – even though, in both instances, the scene only seemed to drive home Trump's desperation.

Of course, he doesn't seem all that worried about looking desperate. Just look at his long-running quest to put his name on things like the Kennedy Center .

He seems focused on crafting the appearance of glory without the hard work and discipline. He'll throw his weight around in hopes of winning laurels, even if the vast majority of other people don't view them as legitimate or deserved.

As recently as this week, Trump said it would be " a great discredit to " the Nobel Committee if he didn't get the award.

His attitude was summed up nicely in a New York Magazine interview last month. Reporter Ben Terris asked the president about Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff's allegation that he is pursuing his own glorification because nobody else will build monuments to him when he's gone.

" That's true ," Trump said. "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will."

articles.title: Trump says Nobel committee not awarding him the peace prize leaves ‘indelible stain’ on Norway
articles.summary: President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.”
articles.body: President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.” Speaking at a rally to boost New York Republicans in Syracuse, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments in office he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having “saved more lives than anyone in history.” Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a U.N. panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza. “I’ve never heard of the person,” Trump said. “I know a lot of people. I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations, anyway. … The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.” “And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump continued. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are antidemocracy and really enemies of civilization, and we will not forget Norway. That you didn’t give this prize with the greatest record in history.” The president added that he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his efforts because he claimed to have ended eight ongoing conflicts. The president did not make mention of the war in Ukraine, which has raged on through his presidency as his administration has failed to bring the conflict to an end. And in the Middle East, the president earlier this year launched a war with Iran that is ongoing. Trump said the committee’s choice to award the prize to Pillay “is just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country.” Throughout his second term, the president has made clear his ambition to secure a Nobel Peace Prize, and his allies have said he deserves it for efforts to end the war in Gaza in addition to other conflicts. Earlier this year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 winner, offered to share her prize with him as she sought his support for her efforts in Venezuela after the Trump administration removed former President Nicolás Maduro from power. After learning of her award at a law gathering in Germany on Friday, Pillay joked to the crowd: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” The president was in Syracuse to boost the candidacy of GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman and state Republicans. He shouted out Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for state attorney general too, before attacking sitting state Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat he has often clashed with. “And on Election Day, New Yorkers should tell both [Gov. Kathy] Hochul and that disgusting Letitia dog — she’s a dog — you’re fired. Get the hell out of here.” The Trump administration has so far failed multiple times in its efforts to prosecute James, who spearheaded an investigation into his business dealings that led to a state judge ruling he had conspired to manipulate his net worth and ordering him to pay a fine of more than $350 million. The fine was later thrown out on appeal by a state court. “Donald Trump is in Syracuse supporting the only attorney general candidate who clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, the man who ended Roe v. Wade,” a James campaign spokesperson said in response to the president’s comments. “The contrast is crystal clear and we welcome it.”

articles.title: Trump rallies New York crowd for Republican Bruce Blakeman's bid to replace Gov. Kathy Hochul
articles.summary: President Donald Trump rallied Syracuse supporters behind Bruce Blakeman's bid to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, promising tax cuts and cheaper energy for New York families.
articles.body: President Donald Trump returned to his home state of New York on Friday night, showcasing America's "New Golden Age" and promising to help Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman flip the Empire State red as the GOP makes its final push toward November's midterm elections. Trump rallied supporters in Syracuse with a sweeping celebration of his administration's economic and immigration agenda, pledging to help New Yorkers secure lower taxes, cheaper energy and safer streets by electing Republicans up and down the ballot. "We're in the Golden Age of America," Trump told the crowd, urging supporters to deliver the same enthusiasm that powered his presidential campaigns. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG "Please pretend I'm on the freaking ballot," Trump urged. "And in a really, in a certain way, I am on the ballot because they can take away everything that we, that we got." The president took Blakeman's challenge to Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul as the centerpiece of the rally, promising direct support from Washington if elected. "[Blakeman will] save this state. He'll turn the state around and I'll help him from the White House," Trump said. "I'll be helping him for governor." Trump blasted Hochul over New York's taxes, utility bills and public safety, arguing that Blakeman could unleash the state's economic potential by embracing domestic energy production and cutting costs for families. DEBRA MESSING SAYS COST OF LIVING, SUBWAY VIOLENCE PUSHED HER TO BACK TRUMP-ENDORSED REPUBLICAN The president also hailed his administration's economic agenda as proof of what Trump described as a remarkable national turnaround. He singled out Micron's planned $100 billion semiconductor complex in central New York, a project the company says is expected to generate 50,000 jobs across the state, including 9,000 directly with Micron. "This will soon be the home to the largest semiconductor manufacturing facility ever built in the Western Hemisphere," Trump said. Blakeman joined Trump onstage and echoed the president's message of a Republican resurgence, promising to cut taxes and utility bills, focus on public safety and make New York more attractive to both businesses and families. "We have to create good jobs, good benefits to keep our young people here," Blakeman said. "We gotta look at business not as the enemy, but as a partner." Trump also threw his support behind Republican congressional candidates Kailee Buller, who is challenging Democrat Rep. John Mannion in New York's 22nd District, and Anthony Constantino, who is running for the state's open 21st District seat, pledging to help Republicans compete for both seats. The rally also notably featured a brief but memorable on-stage appearance by legendary former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson, whom Trump invited up before the crowd. "I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump," Tyson said. "And, there's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump. Thank you. Thank you very much." Trump responded with a laugh, recalling Tyson's notorious reputation. "I don't want to fight him," Trump joked, before complimenting the former champion. "You look good. Mike. What the h— are you doing?" "We're going to elect a Republican House and Republican Senate," Trump said.

articles.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to look at 2016 election lawsuit against Clinton: Report
articles.summary: President Trump asked the Supreme Court on Friday to reopen his dismissed lawsuit against former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, reviving claims that she and other political adversaries orchestrated an effort to sabotage his 2016 presidential campaign by tying it to Russia. Trump filed the appeal after a federal judge dismissed his case and ordered…
articles.body:
President Trump asked the Supreme Court on Friday to reopen his dismissed lawsuit against former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, reviving claims that she and other political adversaries orchestrated an effort to sabotage his 2016 presidential campaign by tying it to Russia.

Trump filed the appeal after a federal judge dismissed his case and ordered the president, as well as his former attorney, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in sanctions. A federal appeals court upheld both rulings last year.

In Friday’s filing, Trump’s attorneys argued the lower courts improperly punished them for pursuing legitimate legal claims, according to Reuters.

As of late Friday night, the lawsuit appeared on the Supreme Court’s online docket system, but the page did not yet list the reported filing. The most recent document available tied to the legal challenge was a late August application requesting more time to file its appeal, which Justice Clarence Thomas approved, extending the deadline to Friday, Oct. 9.

The attorneys wrote that the decision reflected “a deeply troubling trend of federal courts using sanctions and disciplinary threats to punish the president and his lawyers for legitimate legal positions that those courts (erroneously) reject,” per Reuters.

“The court’s intervention is necessary to protect the presidency, and to prevent judicial disagreement from becoming a license to punish its advocates,” the lawyers continued.

Trump first filed the lawsuit in 2022, accusing Clinton, former FBI Director James Comey, the Democratic National Committee and others of conspiring to undermine his presidential bid by bolstering allegations that his campaign colluded with Russia.

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the case in September of that same year, finding Trump’s claims were legally insufficient and that some were filed too late.

Middlebrooks later sanctioned Trump and Habba, describing the lawsuit as a “two-hundred-page political manifesto” and accusing the president, who was not in office at the time of the challenge, of using the courts to advance his political grievances.

The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal and sanctions in 2025. The unanimous three-judge panel, which included Trump appointee Andrew Brasher, found many of lawsuit’s arguments “frivolous.”

The appeal follows Trump’s recent comments that he could have taken action against Clinton, as well as former Presidents Obama and Biden, but chose not to out of respect for the presidency.

“I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden,” Trump told reporters while discussing the possibility of facing another impeachment should Democrats regain control of Congress.

articles.title: Federal judge: DOJ cannot request states’ voter lists for eligibility database
articles.summary: A federal judge struck down on Friday the Justice Department’s nationwide effort to collect voter registration records and identify suspected non-U.S. citizens, blocking the Trump administration from continuing the program even in states that voluntarily cooperated. U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington ruled the department exceeded its legal authority and violated federal privacy laws…
articles.body:
A federal judge struck down on Friday the Justice Department’s nationwide effort to collect voter registration records and identify suspected non-U.S. citizens, blocking the Trump administration from continuing the program even in states that voluntarily cooperated.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington ruled the department exceeded its legal authority and violated federal privacy laws by requesting sensitive voter information and sharing it with other agencies to identify people’s citizenship status.

The 78-page ruling struck down the DOJ’s entire voter list maintenance policy, invalidating it nationwide. The decision came after multiple states similarly won challenges against the Justice Departments rule in their respective jurisdictions.

“DOJ cannot run roughshod over longstanding laws that were carefully crafted to protect the rights of American people,” Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, wrote.

The decision stems from an April lawsuit filed by voting rights group Common Cause and four voters, who accused the administration of attempting to create a “sprawling new voter surveillance and purging apparatus” ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The plaintiffs argued the Justice Department was attempting to seize control of voter registration procedures traditionally overseen by states, putting eligible Americans at risk of being wrongfully removed from voter rolls.

The program began last year following an executive order from President Trump directing federal officials to work with states to identify potential election law violations.

The DOJ subsequently requested unredacted voter registration lists nationwide, seeking sensitive information including names, addresses and partial Social Security numbers.

At least 18 states complied, allowing the department to share their voter records with the Department of Homeland Security and check citizenship status through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database.

Participating states also agreed to remove voters identified as ineligible within 45 days of notification.

Sooknanan found the department failed to adequately consider the risk of mistakenly removing eligible voters despite knowing federal citizenship records contained inaccuracies.

The judge cited a 2006 Social Security Administration audit that found approximately 3.3 million U.S. citizens had been misidentified as noncitizens.

“The Court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more,” Sooknanan wrote.

articles.title: Donald Trump says Nobel Peace Prize decision leaves 'stain' on Norway
articles.summary: The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing".

The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person".

"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget".

Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.

Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize.

Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence.

"The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said.

Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law" , which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.

Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.

Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace".

In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.

Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".

The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable.

"Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time."
